title: Trump Reflects on Midterm Defeats, Admits Deportation Strategy Was 'Too Tough' in Candid Interview
snippet: Following significant Republican midterm losses, President Donald Trump pointed to low supporter turnout, acknowledged messaging stumbles on the economy, and defended his foreign policy in a wide-ranging post-election sit-down.
content:
Following a bruising midterm cycle that saw Republicans lose control of over 40 House seats and key Senate positions, President Donald Trump offered a frank self-assessment in an interview with 60 Minutes. Facing mounting scrutiny over his administration's trajectory, the president stood by his economic stewardship and military decisions while conceding that critical aspects of his messaging and aggressive deportation strategy may have backfired at the ballot box.

Attributing Losses to Turnout and Absence from the Ballot

Addressing the fallout from Tuesday's electoral setback, Trump insisted the main factor behind the GOP's underperformance was simple: his own absence from the top of the ticket. Despite urging supporters ahead of Election Day to act as though he were running, the president acknowledged many core voters ultimately stayed home. "I think they didn't vote, really," Trump noted, adding that high gas prices tied to the ongoing conflict with Iran also dampened voter enthusiasm.

While exit polls showed widespread voter dissatisfaction with the economy and rising costs, Trump maintained that the administration's financial performance has been strong. However, he admitted to a breakdown in communication, characterizing the issue as "bad messaging" that failed to effectively highlight record 401(k) balances and job growth to struggling households.

Immigration Strategy and White House Turnover

In a notable concession, Trump reflected on his signature border enforcement push, admitting that mass deportation efforts may have gone "too tough" by targeting hard-working undocumented immigrants alongside criminal offenders. The shift in tone comes as exit polls indicated a major rebound for Democrats among Latino voters in key battleground states.

The interview coincided with immediate shifts inside the West Wing. Shortly after hinting at forthcoming personnel changes, Trump announced the exit of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. She is set to be succeeded by Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner known for shaping the administration's uncompromising border policies.

Foreign Policy and the Path to 2028

On foreign affairs, Trump pushed back against critics—and internal dissent from Vice President JD Vance—regarding the administration's military campaign against Iran. Framing the strategic degradation of Iran's military and nuclear capabilities as a long-term triumph, Trump compared his historic standing to President Ulysses S. Grant, predicting history would vindicate his posture even if voters penalized it in the short term.

Looking toward the remainder of his term, Trump promised "tremendous numbers of pardons" for administration allies and January 6th defendants, while downplaying speculation over his immediate involvement in picking a 2028 Republican successor. As for his personal legacy and political foes, Trump remained characteristically unfiltered: when asked if he could forgive his opponents, the president replied simply, "I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and always will."
